svg.aria-label: How the same event recorded by three systems in different time zones looks out of order until all timestamps are converted to UTC, which reveals the true sequence.
svg.title: Timestamps and time zones — why you convert everything to UTC before you correlate
svg.text: THE SAME EVENT, THREE SYSTEMS — THE CLOCK LIES UNTIL YOU NORMALISE TO UTC
As recorded — looks out of order
Firewall (UTC) 14:03:11 block outbound
Workstation (EST) 09:03:09 process start
Cloud app (UTC) 14:03:14 data export
If you sort by the raw times, the workstation event
looks like it happened FIVE HOURS earlier — so you'd
wrongly conclude it wasn't part of this incident.
Converted to UTC — the truth
14:03:09 Workstation process start (EST+5)
14:03:11 Firewall block outbound
14:03:14 Cloud app data export
Now the sequence is clear: the process started, tried
to call out (blocked), then data left via the cloud —
a 5-second chain, one incident.
THE RULES THAT KEEP TIME HONEST
• Always convert to UTC before correlating. Different sources log in different zones; a raw sort mixes them and breaks the timeline.
• Watch for clock skew. A host with a wrong clock can misplace events by minutes or hours. NTP keeps clocks synced; drift is itself a data-quality problem.
• Know which time you're reading. Event time (when it happened) vs ingest time (when the SIEM received it) can differ — a delayed log isn't a late attack.
• Record the zone. A timestamp with no zone is ambiguous; "09:03" means nothing until you know 09:03 where.
